items.stem: A company runs order-processing workers on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Several applications send messages to an Amazon SQS standard queue. The workers poll the queue and delete each message after they process it. Processing a message takes up to 4 minutes. The queue uses the default visibility timeout, and many messages are processed by two different workers. Which change will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to a value that is longer than the longest processing time of one message.
options.why: Each message stays [temporarily invisible to other consumers](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-receive-keeps-message-hidden) for the whole processing time, so a second worker does not receive it.

options.text: Create a dead-letter queue, and add a redrive policy to the queue that moves a message after several unsuccessful receives.
options.why: A dead-letter queue sets aside messages that keep failing; it does not stop a second worker from receiving a message that is still in progress.
options.misconception: A dead-letter queue stops a second consumer from receiving a message that is still in progress.

options.text: Change the workers to call ChangeMessageVisibility during processing, so that each message stays hidden until the worker finishes with it.
options.why: It works, but every worker needs new code for each message, although one queue setting gives the same result.
options.misconception: Extends the timeout in worker code when one queue setting is enough.

options.text: Change the workers to count the receives of each message and to move a message that keeps failing to a second queue.
options.why: The messages do not fail; they come back because the timeout ends too early, so counting receives does not stop the duplicates.
options.misconception: Treats the duplicate deliveries as messages that keep failing.

items.explanation: Processing takes as long as 4 minutes, but the default visibility timeout is [30 seconds](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-visibility-timeout-default). If the timeout ends before the delete, the message [becomes visible again in the queue](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-undeleted-message-visible-again), and [a duplicate message is received by another consumer](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-visibility-timeout-too-short-gives-duplicate). One queue setting that is longer than the processing time keeps each message hidden until its worker deletes it.
items.takeaway: Set the visibility timeout longer than the longest processing time, or a second consumer receives the message.
items.twin: If the stem said "A few malformed messages fail every time" instead: a dead-letter queue, because a redrive policy counts the [number of times a consumer can receive](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning) a message.
items.say: The timeout ends before the worker deletes the message, so I'd raise the visibility timeout above the processing time.

solvers.stem_only: The default visibility timeout (30 seconds) is shorter than the 4-minute processing time, so messages reappear and a second worker takes them; raise the queue's visibility timeout above the longest processing time.

items.stem: A company runs a consumer application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application receives messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue and writes the results to a database. A developer finds a bug: the application processes each message successfully, but the code that calls the DeleteMessage action never runs. The queue uses its default settings. What happens to a message after the application receives and processes it?
keywords: the code that calls the DeleteMessage action never runs
The queue uses its default settings

options.text: Amazon SQS deleted the message when the application received it, so the bug has no effect on the queue.
options.why: A received message is [temporarily invisible to other consumers](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-receive-keeps-message-hidden), but it stays in the queue until a consumer deletes it.

options.text: The message stays hidden from all consumers until the retention period of the queue ends, and then Amazon SQS deletes the message from the queue.
options.why: The message is hidden for the visibility timeout, not for the retention period; after the timeout it [becomes visible again in the queue](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-undeleted-message-visible-again).
options.misconception: the visibility timeout lasts as long as the retention period

options.text: The message stays in the queue, and it becomes visible again when the visibility timeout ends, so a consumer receives it again.
options.why: The message was never deleted, so it [becomes visible again in the queue](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-undeleted-message-visible-again) after the visibility timeout, and a consumer processes it a second time.

options.text: Amazon SQS moves the message to a dead-letter queue when the visibility timeout ends, so no consumer receives it again.
options.why: A move to a dead-letter queue comes from a redrive policy, after the [number of times a consumer can receive](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning) the message, not after one timeout.

items.explanation: Receiving a message does not remove it: [it remains in the queue](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-receive-keeps-message-hidden) and is hidden from other consumers for the visibility timeout. A consumer removes it with a separate call: [you explicitly delete messages](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-manual-delete-after-processing) with DeleteMessage. Without that call, the message returns to the queue and is processed again.
items.takeaway: Receiving hides a message, and [you explicitly delete messages](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-manual-delete-after-processing) with DeleteMessage.
items.twin: If the stem said "the application calls DeleteMessage after it processes each message" instead: the message is removed, because [you explicitly delete messages](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-manual-delete-after-processing) with that call.
items.say: Receiving only hides the message; if nobody deletes it, it comes back when the visibility timeout ends.

solvers.stem_only: Receiving a message does not delete it. The message is hidden for the visibility timeout; when the timeout ends without a DeleteMessage call it becomes visible again and is received and processed again, repeatedly, until the retention period ends (no DLQ by default).

items.stem: A company sends account events for many customers to Amazon SQS. The events of each customer must be processed exactly once and in the order they were sent. Events of different customers must be processed in parallel by many consumers, so that a slow customer does not delay the others. Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: processed exactly once and in the order they were sent
Events of different customers must be processed in parallel

options.text: Give each event a random message group ID, because the FIFO queue keeps one order across all of its messages.
options.why: Order holds inside a group, but [messages with different message group IDs](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-no-order-across-groups) can arrive or be processed out of order, so random IDs break each customer's order.

options.text: Use an Amazon SQS standard queue, because a standard queue delivers each message once and in the order it was sent.
options.why: A standard queue gives [at-least-once message delivery](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates), so [more than one copy of a message](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates) can arrive.

options.text: Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, and have the producers send the account events of all customers to that one queue.
options.why: A FIFO queue gives [exactly-once processing](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-fifo-exactly-once-processing), and one queue serves every customer without extra queues to manage.

options.text: Create a separate Amazon SQS FIFO queue for each customer, and run a dedicated group of consumers for each of those queues.
options.why: It works, but every new customer needs a new queue and new consumers, while one queue with a group for each customer does the same job.
options.misconception: parallel work needs a separate queue for each customer

options.text: Set the message group ID of each event to the ID of the customer that the event belongs to.
options.why: Order is strict [within a message group ID](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group), and different groups allow [parallel processing of messages](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-groups-processed-in-parallel) by many consumers.

items.explanation: A FIFO queue gives [exactly-once processing](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-fifo-exactly-once-processing). The message group ID decides the rest: order is kept [within a message group ID](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group), and the queue allows parallel work [across different message group IDs](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-groups-processed-in-parallel). With the customer ID as the group ID, each customer keeps its order, and many consumers work on different customers at the same time.
items.takeaway: In a FIFO queue, the message group ID sets the unit of order and the unit of parallel work.
items.twin: If the stem said "all events must be processed in one strict order" instead: use one message group ID for all events, because order is strict [within a message group ID](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group).
items.say: One FIFO queue, and the customer ID as the message group ID: order per customer, parallel across customers.

solvers.stem_only: Use one SQS FIFO queue (exactly-once processing, ordering) and set the message group ID to the customer ID, so order holds per customer while different groups are consumed in parallel.

items.stem: A company is building an event-driven platform for its online store. Services that several teams own must react to events, and each service needs only some of the events. The teams do not want to write or run routing code. The events come from AWS services, from the company's own applications, and from a SaaS partner's application. Each service selects events by fields inside the event detail. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: by fields inside the event detail

options.text: Write the events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream, and have every service read all records of the stream and discard the events that it does not need.
options.why: A stream is built for [real-time processing of streaming big data](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-kinesis-streams-realtime-and-replay); every service would need its own code to read and filter events that a rule matches for it.
options.misconception: a data stream is the managed way to route events to many services

options.text: Send the events to one Amazon SQS queue, and have every service poll the queue and discard the events that it does not need.
options.why: A queue serves [a single subscriber typically](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss): services that poll one queue split the events, so each service misses events it needs.

options.text: Send the events to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, and create one rule for each service with an event pattern that matches the events it needs.
options.why: EventBridge takes events from all three kinds of sources, and each rule's pattern can test [event metadata, and/or event detail values](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-pattern-matches-metadata-data-content).

options.text: Publish the events to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe each service to the topic with a filter policy that matches the events it needs.
options.why: EventBridge is the [only event-based service](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners) with a direct SaaS partner link, so the SaaS events would need extra parts before they reach the topic.

items.explanation: The SaaS source decides it: EventBridge is the [only event-based service](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners) that integrates directly with [third-party SaaS partners](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners). The [default event bus](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events) also [automatically receives events from AWS services](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events), and a rule for each service selects events by fields in the event detail, with no routing code.
items.takeaway: Events from AWS services, your applications and SaaS partners, matched on content: an EventBridge event bus with rules.
items.twin: If the stem said "All events come from the company's own order application. Every event must also reach the mobile phones of thousands of field agents by SMS" instead: an SNS topic with filter policies.
items.say: SaaS events plus AWS events plus content matching: that is an EventBridge event bus with one rule per service.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon EventBridge: an event bus receives AWS service events, custom application events and SaaS partner events; one rule per service with an event pattern on detail fields routes events with no routing code.

items.stem: A company uses an Amazon SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue. Both queues keep the default message retention period. A message moves to the dead-letter queue after it fails several times, usually within one hour of the first send. Failed messages disappear from the dead-letter queue before the support team reviews them. The company must retain each failed message for at least 10 days after it was first sent. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Both queues keep the default message retention period
at least 10 days after it was first sent

options.text: Set the message retention period of the source queue to 14 days, and keep the retention period of the dead-letter queue at its default.
options.why: The messages leave the source queue within an hour; the dead-letter queue still deletes them [4 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-default) after the first send.
options.misconception: the source queue's retention controls a message after it moves

options.text: Set the message retention period of the dead-letter queue to 14 days, and keep the retention period of the source queue unchanged.
options.why: The dead-letter queue's own retention deletes the failed messages, and [14 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-range) after the first send covers the 10 days.

options.text: Lower the maximum receives of the redrive policy, so that failed messages move sooner and get more time in the dead-letter queue.
options.why: In a standard queue [the enqueue timestamp is unchanged](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-standard-enqueue-timestamp-unchanged) by the move, so an earlier move gives no extra time.

options.text: Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that copies the messages in the dead-letter queue to an Amazon S3 bucket every day.
options.why: It works, but the company writes and runs copy code when one queue setting keeps the messages long enough.
options.misconception: a queue cannot keep messages long enough, so they need a second store

items.explanation: In a standard queue, [the enqueue timestamp is unchanged](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-standard-enqueue-timestamp-unchanged) when a message moves, so the dead-letter queue counts its retention from the first send. Its default of [4 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-default) is too short. AWS advises a dead-letter queue retention [longer than the retention period](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-retention-longer-than-source-queue) of the source queue, and the maximum of [14 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-range) covers 10 days.
items.takeaway: A dead-letter queue counts retention from the first send, so give it the longer retention.
items.twin: If the stem said "for at least 30 days after it was first sent" instead: copy the failed messages to Amazon S3, because a queue keeps a message for at most [14 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-range).
items.say: The move does not reset the clock, so I raise the retention of the dead-letter queue itself to fourteen days.

solvers.stem_only: For a standard queue, a message keeps its original enqueue timestamp when it moves to the dead-letter queue, so the DLQ retention period must cover 10 days from first send: raise the DLQ retention (to the 14-day maximum); the source queue can stay as is because messages leave it within an hour.

items.stem: A company publishes order events to a custom Amazon EventBridge event bus. A rule on the bus sends the events to an AWS Lambda function. Last week, a bug made the function process orders wrongly for several hours. After the fix, the company could not process those events again. After any future bug, the company must be able to process the events of the last 30 days again. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: process orders wrongly for several hours
process the events of the last 30 days again

options.text: After each fix, configure the Lambda function to read the events of the affected time window again from the custom event bus.
options.why: EventBridge [doesn't persist events](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-decision-no-persistence-at-least-once), so the bus has no past events for the function to read.

options.text: Configure an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue for the rule target, and after each fix send the events in that dead-letter queue to the function again.
options.why: A target's dead-letter queue stores [events that couldn't successfully be delivered](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-dlq-is-standard-sqs-queue); these events were delivered, and the function processed them wrongly.

options.text: Add a rule that sends every event through Amazon Data Firehose to Amazon S3, and write a tool that publishes the stored events again.
options.why: It works, but the company builds and runs a copy pipeline and a resend tool that an archive and a replay already provide.
options.misconception: past events can be sent again only with a custom store and tool

options.text: Create an archive of the event bus that keeps events for 30 days, and after each fix start a replay of the affected time window.
options.why: The archive keeps the events for the days you set, and a replay sends the events of the chosen window back to the bus.

items.explanation: The bus keeps nothing by itself: EventBridge [doesn't persist events](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-decision-no-persistence-at-least-once). An archive keeps them, and you set the [days to retain events in the archive](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-archive-retention-indefinite-by-default). After a fix, a replay lets you [reprocess past events](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-event-replay-reprocesses-past-events-to-bus-or-rule) of the affected window, and the rule sends them to the fixed function.
items.takeaway: To process EventBridge events again later, archive them first and replay them after the fix.
items.twin: If the stem said "the rule could not deliver the events to the function" instead: a dead-letter queue on the target, because it stores [events that couldn't successfully be delivered](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-dlq-is-standard-sqs-queue).
items.say: The bus keeps nothing, so I archive the events and replay the bad window after the fix.

solvers.stem_only: Create an EventBridge archive on the custom bus with 30-day retention, and use EventBridge replay for the affected time window after a fix.

items.stem: An Amazon SNS standard topic delivers order events to a partner's HTTPS endpoint and to an Amazon SQS queue of the company. The partner endpoint is sometimes unavailable for several hours, and the events for the partner are lost. The company must keep each undelivered event for the partner so that it can send the event again later. Which combination of actions meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: keep each undelivered event for the partner

options.text: Attach an Amazon SQS queue as the dead-letter queue of the SNS topic itself, so that the queue catches the failed deliveries of every subscription of the topic.
options.why: A topic has no dead-letter queue, because [message deliveries happen at the subscription level](../facts/sns.md#sns-dlq-attached-to-subscription-not-topic).

options.text: Create an Amazon SQS standard queue in the same AWS account and Region as the partner's subscription, with a policy that allows the topic to send.
options.why: The dead-letter queue must be in the [same AWS account and Region](../facts/sns.md#sns-dlq-same-account-and-region-as-subscription) as the subscription, and SNS sends to it after you [set a policy on the Amazon SQS queue](../facts/sns.md#sns-sqs-queue-needs-policy-allowing-topic).

options.text: Change the delivery policy of the HTTPS subscription so that Amazon SNS keeps retrying each failed delivery to the partner endpoint for 24 hours.
options.why: The total retry time of an HTTP/S delivery policy cannot exceed [3,600 seconds](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-http-total-retry-time-max), so the topic cannot hold an event for a whole day.

options.text: Replace the HTTPS subscription with an AWS Lambda function that calls the partner endpoint and stores each failed event in Amazon S3.
options.why: It works, but the company writes and runs delivery and retry code that a dead-letter queue on the subscription already gives.
options.misconception: keeping failed deliveries needs custom delivery code

options.text: Attach an Amazon SQS standard queue as the dead-letter queue of the partner's HTTPS subscription, and send the stored events again when the partner is back.
options.why: Deliveries happen per subscription, so the dead-letter queue is [attached to an Amazon SNS subscription](../facts/sns.md#sns-dlq-attached-to-subscription-not-topic) and keeps the partner's failed events for a later resend.

items.explanation: When its retries end, SNS [stops retrying the delivery and discards the message](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-exhausted-discards-unless-dlq) unless [a dead-letter queue is attached to the subscription](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-exhausted-discards-unless-dlq). So the company creates a standard queue that SNS can write to and attaches it to the partner's subscription. The queue keeps each undelivered event until the company sends it again.
items.takeaway: An SNS dead-letter queue belongs to one subscription, in the same account and Region.
items.twin: If the stem said "each event must wait in a queue until the partner pulls it" instead: subscribe an SQS queue for the partner, which prevents loss [when subscribers are offline](../facts/sns.md#sns-with-sqs-prevents-loss-for-offline-subscribers).
items.say: SNS drops a message when its retries end, so I attach a dead-letter queue to the partner's subscription.

solvers.stem_only: Give the HTTPS subscription (not the topic) a redrive policy with an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue. The DLQ must be a standard queue (standard topic) in the same account and Region as the subscription, and its queue policy must let the SNS topic send messages. Undelivered events land there after SNS retries run out and can be replayed later. Longer retry policies do not help: HTTP/S retries are capped well below several hours of outage handling and do not store events.

items.stem: A company runs the sign-up process of its web application on AWS Lambda. The company must send a reminder email to each new user 3 days after the user signs up. Each reminder is a one-time action for that user, and many users sign up every day. An existing Lambda function already sends one reminder email when it is invoked with a user ID. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: 3 days after the user signs up

options.text: When a user signs up, send the user ID to an Amazon SQS delay queue with a delay of 3 days, and have the reminder function read the queue.
options.why: A delay queue holds a message for at most [15 minutes](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-delay-queue-range), so a delay of 3 days is not possible.

options.text: Run a cron job on an Amazon EC2 instance every hour that reads the user table and invokes the reminder function for users who signed up 3 days ago.
options.why: It works, but the company patches and runs an instance and writes scanning code for a job that a schedule does by itself.
options.misconception: timed jobs need a server that runs a cron table

options.text: When a user signs up, create an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedule that invokes the reminder function with the user ID 3 days later.
options.why: A one-time schedule [invokes a target only once](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-scheduler-one-time-schedule-invokes-once), at the time set during sign-up, with no server and no polling code.

options.text: When a user signs up, send the user ID to an Amazon SQS queue with a message timer of 3 days, and have the reminder function read the queue.
options.why: A message timer has the same limit as a delay queue: at most [15 minutes](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-timer-range) for each message.

items.explanation: SQS delay queues and message timers schedule delivery [up to 15 minutes in the future](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-eventbridge-scheduler-for-advanced-scheduling), far short of 3 days. For longer waits, [EventBridge Scheduler is the recommended solution](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-eventbridge-scheduler-for-advanced-scheduling). A one-time schedule per user [invokes a target only once](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-scheduler-one-time-schedule-invokes-once), at the reminder time, and nothing runs in between.
items.takeaway: A wait longer than [15 minutes](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-delay-queue-range) is a job for EventBridge Scheduler, not for an SQS delay.
items.twin: If the stem said "10 minutes after the user signs up" instead: an SQS delay queue fits, because it delays delivery for at most [15 minutes](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-delay-queue-range).
items.say: SQS can delay a message for fifteen minutes at most, so for three days I create a one-time schedule in EventBridge Scheduler.

solvers.stem_only: Create an EventBridge Scheduler one-time (at) schedule per user that invokes the existing function 3 days later; SQS delays are limited to 15 minutes, so a queue delay cannot do it.

items.stem: A company runs an order API on Amazon EC2 instances. The API sends each order directly to the order service, which writes the order to a relational database. During sales, the database cannot keep up, requests time out, and orders are lost. Only the company's order service processes the orders. The order service must process every order, even after it has been offline for a few hours. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Only the company's order service processes the orders
even after it has been offline for a few hours

options.text: Have the API send each order to one Amazon SQS queue, and have each service that processes orders poll that queue and process the orders it receives.
options.why: One queue holds every order until the order service processes it, and the order service writes to the database at its own pace.

options.text: Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for each service that processes orders, and have each service poll its queue.
options.why: It works, but SNS is for [fanout notifications](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-typical-use), and with one consumer the topic is an extra part with nothing to fan out to.
options.misconception: adds a topic in front of the queue when only one service consumes the orders

options.text: Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe the HTTPS endpoint of each service that processes orders so that each service receives every order.
options.why: In SNS, [messages are not persisted](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-no-persistence), and HTTPS retries end within [3,600 seconds](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-http-total-retry-time-max), so an outage of a few hours loses orders.

options.text: Move the database to a larger instance class, and add a read replica so that the database can take more of the load during sales.
options.why: A larger database still takes every write at the moment of the peak, and it holds no order while the order service is offline.
options.misconception: a larger database removes the need for a buffer between the API and the database

items.explanation: One service consumes the orders, so one queue is enough. SQS is built for [buffering requests](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-decision-typical-use): the database receives orders at the pace of the order service. Each order stays in the queue [until successfully processed or expired](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-decision-keeps-until-processed), and the default retention of [4 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-default) covers an outage of a few hours.
items.takeaway: One consumer and a database that falls behind: put one SQS queue in front of the database.
items.twin: If the stem said "The order service, the shipping service and the analytics service must each process every order" instead: an SNS topic with one SQS queue for each service, because each queue keeps its own copy.
items.say: One consumer, so one queue: SQS buffers the orders, and the order service writes them at its own pace.

solvers.stem_only: Put one SQS queue between the API and the single order service to buffer orders; the queue retains messages (days) while the service is offline and lets it consume at its own pace. No fan-out is needed for one consumer.

items.stem: A company is splitting an application into microservices. When a customer places an order, the order service creates an order event. The billing, shipping and email microservices must each receive every order event at the same time, and each microservice handles the event in its own way. The order service must not wait for the other microservices or know their addresses. Which AWS service provides this publish/subscribe model?
keywords: must each receive every order event at the same time

options.text: One Amazon SQS standard queue that the order service sends each event to, polled by all three microservices
options.why: A queue serves [a single subscriber typically](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss): the three microservices split the events between them, and none of them receives every event.

options.text: One Amazon SQS FIFO queue that the order service sends each event to, with one message group ID per microservice
options.why: A message group ID orders messages inside one queue; each message still goes to one consumer, so the order service would have to send three copies itself.
options.misconception: message group IDs give each consumer its own copy of every message

options.text: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, with one schedule for each microservice that passes on the new order events
options.why: EventBridge Scheduler runs [rate-based, cron-based, and one-time schedules](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-scheduler-three-schedule-types): a schedule starts at a set time, not when an order event appears.
options.misconception: a scheduler forwards events as they happen

options.text: An Amazon SNS topic that the order service publishes each event to, with one subscription for each microservice
options.why: A published message goes to [all applicable subscribers](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-publish-triggers-delivery-to-all-subscribers) of the topic, so each microservice gets its own copy of every event.

items.explanation: Publish/subscribe is the job of SNS: it is built for [pub/sub messaging](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-typical-use). When the order service publishes an event to the topic, SNS delivers it to [all applicable subscribers](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-publish-triggers-delivery-to-all-subscribers) at once. The order service knows the topic, not the microservices, and each microservice has its own subscription.
items.takeaway: Every consumer needs every message: publish to an SNS topic, not to one shared queue.
items.twin: If the stem said "each order event must be handled by one of three identical workers" instead: one SQS queue, because a queue serves [a single subscriber typically](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss).
items.say: Every service needs every event, so I publish to an SNS topic and give each service a subscription.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon SNS topic with one subscription per microservice (pub/sub fan-out); the publisher does not know subscribers.

verification.note: exam-05: the stem names the answer's category (publish/subscribe model) and trains keyword matching; replaced in the shipped set by q011, q021 and q006 (exam-02)

items.stem: A company is building an event-driven platform for its online store. Services that several teams own must react to events, and each service needs only some of the events. The teams do not want to write or run routing code. All events come from the company's own order application. Every event must also reach the mobile phones of thousands of field agents by SMS within seconds. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: All events come from the company's own order application
mobile phones of thousands of field agents by SMS

options.text: Write the events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream, and have every service read all records of the stream and discard the events that it does not need.
options.why: A stream is built for [real-time processing of streaming big data](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-kinesis-streams-realtime-and-replay); each service needs its own filter code, and the SMS messages still need another service.
options.misconception: a data stream is the managed way to route events to many services

options.text: Send the events to one Amazon SQS queue, and have every service poll the queue and discard the events that it does not need.
options.why: A queue serves [a single subscriber typically](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss): services that poll one queue split the events, and a queue sends no SMS.

options.text: Send the events to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, and create one rule for each service with an event pattern that matches the events it needs.
options.why: It works for the services, but the SMS messages still need an SNS topic as a rule target: two services where SNS alone covers both needs.
options.misconception: an event bus is the better router even when every event comes from one application

options.text: Publish the events to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe each service to the topic with a filter policy that matches the events it needs.
options.why: Each service filters with [subscription filter policies](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-filter-policies), and the agents' phone numbers subscribe to the same topic without a filter.

items.explanation: One service covers both needs. An SNS topic delivers to [mobile applications, mobile phone numbers, and email addresses](../facts/sns.md#sns-a2p-subscriber-types) as well as to services, and SNS is recommended for [thousands or millions of endpoints](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-sns-recommended-for-high-fan-out-thousands-or-millions). Each service picks its events with a filter policy, and the field agents' phones receive every event.
items.takeaway: Events from your own application that also go to many phones: an SNS topic with filter policies.
items.twin: If the stem said "The events come from AWS services, from the company's own applications, and from a SaaS partner's application" instead: an EventBridge event bus, because it integrates directly with [third-party SaaS partners](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners).
items.say: One source and thousands of phones by SMS: an SNS topic, with filter policies for the services.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon SNS: one topic, subscription filter policies per service, and SNS also delivers SMS to many phone numbers natively; EventBridge cannot send SMS without an extra SNS hop.

items.stem: A company's payment service reads orders from an Amazon SQS standard queue and charges the customer for each order. Each order has a unique order ID. Sometimes a customer is charged twice for one order. Logs show two causes: some orders are received twice from the queue, and a partner system sometimes sends the same order again several hours later. Which solution will BEST prevent duplicate charges?
keywords: sends the same order again several hours later

options.text: Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to its maximum value, so that a second consumer cannot receive an order that is still in progress.
options.why: A standard queue can deliver [more than one copy of a message](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates) for other reasons too, and the partner repeats are new messages that no timeout stops.
options.misconception: A long visibility timeout removes every duplicate of a standard queue.

options.text: Replace the standard queue with an SQS FIFO queue that uses content-based deduplication, and keep the code of the payment service unchanged.
options.why: It removes repeats only inside the [5 minute deduplication interval](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-deduplication-interval-5-minutes), so partner orders that arrive hours later are still charged twice.

options.text: Make the payment service record each order ID with a conditional write before it charges, and skip an order whose ID is already recorded.
options.why: The order ID is the token, and consumers should [keep track of each token received](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-consumers-keep-idempotency-tokens-ignore-duplicates), which stops both causes of duplicate charges.

options.text: Keep the standard queue and fix the partner system alone, because a standard queue delivers each message exactly once and in order.
options.why: A standard queue gives [at-least-once message delivery](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates), so the queue itself also repeats some orders.

items.explanation: Duplicates come from two places, so the fix belongs in the consumer. With a standard queue you must [design your applications to be idempotent](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-standard-queue-design-idempotent-consumers). A conditional write of the order ID lets the payment service charge each order a single time, whether the repeat comes from the queue or from the partner.
items.takeaway: When duplicates come from several sources, make the consumer idempotent with a record of each processed ID.
items.twin: If the stem said "all duplicates come from the queue, and the payment code cannot change" instead: a FIFO queue, because [duplicates are not introduced into the queue](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-fifo-exactly-once-processing).
items.say: Duplicates come from the queue and from the partner, so I'd make the consumer idempotent on the order ID.

solvers.stem_only: Make the consumer idempotent: record the order ID with a conditional write (for example in DynamoDB) before charging and skip IDs already seen; FIFO deduplication only covers a 5-minute window, so it cannot catch a resend hours later.

items.stem: A company must react whenever any Amazon EC2 instance in its AWS account changes to the stopped state. The operations team must receive an email within a few minutes, and an existing AWS Lambda function must create a ticket for each stopped instance. Instances are stopped by users in the console, by scripts and by scheduled jobs. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a Lambda function that runs every minute, calls DescribeInstances, compares the states with the last run, and sends the email and the ticket.
options.why: It works, but it is polling code to run and fix, although the default bus [automatically receives events from AWS services](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events).

options.text: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that writes to an Amazon S3 bucket, and add an S3 event notification that invokes a function to read each log file.
options.why: It works, but it adds a trail, a bucket and log-parsing code, which is far more to run than one rule on the event bus.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the StatusCheckFailed metric of each instance, and send the alarm notifications to an Amazon SNS topic with an email subscription.
options.why: Status checks find problems that [require your involvement to repair](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-status-check-instance-needs-you) or [require AWS involvement to repair](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-status-check-system-needs-aws); a requested stop is a state change, not a failed check.
options.misconception: A status check alarm reports every stop of an instance.

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for EC2 stop events, with the Lambda function and an email-subscribed SNS topic as targets.
options.why: The rule matches the stop events on the [default event bus](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events) and can [route to multiple targets](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-single-rule-routes-to-multiple-targets-in-parallel), so one rule reaches both the topic and the function.

items.explanation: Every account has a [default event bus](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events) that [automatically receives events from AWS services](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events), and EC2 is one of those services. One rule matches the stopped state, whoever stopped the instance. A single rule can [route to multiple targets](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-single-rule-routes-to-multiple-targets-in-parallel), so the topic sends the email and the function creates the ticket, with no code to poll.
items.takeaway: To react to a change of an AWS resource, match its event with an EventBridge rule; do not poll.
items.twin: If the stem said "must react when the instance health checks fail" instead: a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed, because failed checks are a metric, not a state change.
items.say: EC2 sends its state changes to the default event bus, so one EventBridge rule with two targets does it without code.

solvers.stem_only: An Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus that matches the EC2 Instance State-change Notification event with state 'stopped'. Targets: the existing Lambda function and an SNS topic with an email subscription. This catches every stop source (console, scripts, schedules) with no polling and no custom code.

docs/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/monitoring-system-instance-status-check#System status checks monitor the AWS sys
docs/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/monitoring-system-instance-status-check#When a status check fails, the correspon

items.stem: A company processes uploaded images with Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances poll an Amazon SQS queue. Each message takes about the same time to process. The number of uploads changes during the day, and each image must be processed within a set time after upload. The group uses target tracking on average CPU utilization, and messages often wait too long. Which metric should the target tracking policy use to BEST meet the processing-time goal?
keywords: Each message takes about the same time to process
The number of uploads changes during the day

options.text: The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric of the queue alone, with one fixed target number of visible messages for the whole group.
options.why: The queue length [might not change proportionally](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-queue-length-not-proportional) to the size of the group, so one fixed target misses the processing-time goal.

options.text: A metric math expression that divides ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible by GroupInServiceInstances, with the acceptable backlog per instance as the target value.
options.why: The [backlog per instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance) shows how much waiting work each instance carries, so its target follows the processing-time goal.

options.text: The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible metric of the queue, with one fixed target number of messages that the instances are processing.
options.why: It counts messages [received but not yet deleted or expired](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-not-visible-messages-is-in-flight): the work in progress, not the messages that wait.

options.text: The NumberOfMessagesSent metric of the queue, with a target value that matches the average number of uploads in one minute.
options.why: It counts the messages that producers add to the queue, so it shows arrivals and not the waiting work of each instance.
options.misconception: The number of arriving messages shows how long messages wait.

items.explanation: The goal is a wait time, and every message takes about the same time, so the signal is the waiting work of each instance. Metric math divides [ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math) by [GroupInServiceInstances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math). Target tracking then keeps the [backlog per instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance) at the acceptable value as the load changes.
items.takeaway: Scale queue workers on the backlog per instance, not on CPU or on the queue length alone.
items.twin: If the stem said "alarm when messages wait too long" instead: [ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-age-of-oldest-message-measures-lag), because it reports the oldest unprocessed message.
items.say: I'd scale on backlog per instance: visible messages divided by the instances in service, with the acceptable backlog as the target.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the metric that target tracking should use to BEST meet a processing-time goal.
I mark the constraints: the instances poll an SQS queue, each message takes about the same time, the number of uploads changes during the day, and messages wait too long with scaling on CPU.
Before I look at the options, I predict the backlog per instance: the visible messages divided by the instances in service, because that number tells how long each instance needs to clear its share.

I remove ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible, because it counts messages that were received but not yet deleted, the work in progress. I remove NumberOfMessagesSent, because new arrivals do not show how much work waits for each instance.

Between the visible messages alone and the visible messages per instance the difference is the size of the group; the stem says the load changes, and the queue length might not change proportionally to the group, so I choose the backlog per instance.
Check: the metric math option follows the waiting work of each instance, adapts to the changing load and serves the processing-time goal. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Target tracking on backlog per instance: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible divided by the number of in-service instances, with the acceptable backlog per instance (latency goal / processing time per message) as the target.

items.stem: A company publishes every order event to an Amazon SNS standard topic. Each message has a message attribute that holds the order type. Two Amazon SQS queues are subscribed to the topic. A Lambda function is also subscribed: it receives every event and copies the return events into a third queue, the returns queue. The company wants to remove the function, and the returns queue must still receive only the return events. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: message attribute that holds the order type

options.text: Subscribe the returns queue to the topic directly, and give that subscription a filter policy that matches the order type of return events.
options.why: SNS sends a message to the subscription when its attributes [satisfy the conditions specified in the filter policy](../facts/sns.md#sns-filter-nonmatching-message-not-sent), so no code is needed.

options.text: Keep a Lambda function between the topic and the returns queue, because an SNS topic sends every message to every subscription.
options.why: A subscriber gets every message by default, but you can [assign a filter policy to the topic subscription](../facts/sns.md#sns-filter-default-every-message) instead of a function.

options.text: Create a separate SNS topic for each order type, change the publishers to send each event to its topic, and subscribe the returns queue to one.
options.why: It works, but every publisher changes, although one filter policy on a subscription to the existing topic gives the same result.

options.text: Replace the topic with an Amazon EventBridge event bus, create one rule for each queue, and change the publishers to send events to the bus.
options.why: It works, but publishers and consumers move to a new service, although the topic already offers [subscription filter policies](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-filter-policies).

items.explanation: Subscribers can [selectively receive only a subset](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-message-filtering-subscribers-receive-subset) of the topic's messages. The order type is already a message attribute, so a filter policy on the returns queue's subscription does the function's work. The publishers, the topic and the other two queues do not change.
items.takeaway: To give one subscriber a subset of a topic's messages, put a filter policy on its subscription.
items.twin: If the stem said "events also come from a SaaS partner application" instead: an EventBridge event bus with rules, because EventBridge integrates directly with [third-party SaaS partners](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners).
items.say: A filter policy on the returns queue's subscription does the function's job, and nothing else changes.

solvers.stem_only: Subscribe the returns queue directly to the SNS topic with a subscription filter policy on the order-type message attribute; remove the function.

items.stem: A company uses an AWS Lambda function to process messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue. The event source mapping uses a batch size of 10, and the queue has a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue. When one message in a batch is malformed, the function returns an error for the whole batch. The other nine messages are processed again and again, and at last all ten messages move to the dead-letter queue. Which solution will retry only the malformed message in the MOST operationally efficient way?
keywords: returns an error for the whole batch

options.text: Change the function to delete each message that it processes without error from the queue, and then return an error for the batch when one message fails.
options.why: It works, but the company writes and runs delete calls for each good message, which the built-in partial batch response replaces with one returned list of failed IDs.
options.misconception: Deleting the good messages in the function code is the efficient way to keep them from a retry.

options.text: Configure an on-failure destination for the function that sends the records of failed invocations to a second SQS queue for review.
options.why: For a queue, the [visibility timeout and redrive policy](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue) on the source queue decide retries and failed messages, not a setting of the function.

options.text: Lower the visibility timeout of the queue so that a failed batch returns to the function sooner and the good messages finish faster.
options.why: A shorter timeout returns the whole batch sooner; it does not separate the malformed message from the nine good ones.

options.text: Turn on ReportBatchItemFailures in the event source mapping, and change the function to return the IDs of the messages that failed.
options.why: With [ReportBatchItemFailures](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response), Lambda can [make only the failed messages visible again](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response), so the good messages are not retried.

items.explanation: A function error returns the whole batch to the queue, so the nine good messages come back with the bad one. With a [partial batch response](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response), the function reports which messages failed. The good messages are not processed again, and the queue's redrive policy moves the malformed message to the dead-letter queue.
items.takeaway: For Lambda with SQS, turn on ReportBatchItemFailures so that one bad message does not send a whole batch back.
items.twin: If the stem said "without any change to the function code" instead: set the batch size of the event source mapping to 1, because a partial batch response needs the function to return the failed message IDs.
items.say: I'd turn on a partial batch response, so the function reports the one failed message and the rest are done.

solvers.stem_only: Turn on partial batch responses: set FunctionResponseTypes to ReportBatchItemFailures on the SQS event source mapping and have the function return batchItemFailures with the message IDs that failed. Lambda then deletes the successful messages and only the malformed one returns to the queue and, after maxReceiveCount, moves to the dead-letter queue.

citations: docs/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async-configuring#When an invocation event exceeds the max
docs/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-errorhandling#With this setting, your function can ret

solvers.flag: Option D (delete each successfully processed message, then return an error) also leaves only the malformed message to be retried, so a careful candidate could defend it; only the phrase 'MOST operationally efficient' (extra SQS API calls and permissions in code versus a mapping setting) separates A from D.

items.stem: An Amazon SNS standard topic and an Amazon SQS standard queue are in the same AWS account. A developer used the Subscribe API action to subscribe the queue to the topic. Server-side encryption is turned off for the queue, and the queue still has the access policy that it had when it was created. Messages published to the topic never arrive in the queue. Which change will deliver the messages in the MOST secure way?
keywords: the queue still has the access policy that it had when it was created

options.text: Add a statement to the queue's access policy that allows every principal (*) to call sqs:SendMessage on the queue, with no condition.
options.why: It works, but a wildcard principal grants access to all users, [including anonymous users (public access)](../facts/iam.md#iam-principal-wildcard-is-public), so any sender can write to the queue.
options.misconception: Opening the queue to every principal is an acceptable fix for a missing delivery permission.

options.text: Add a statement to the queue's access policy that allows the SNS service principal to call sqs:SendMessage, with an aws:SourceArn condition for the topic.
options.why: The statement names the SNS service as sender, and the [aws:SourceArn condition](../facts/sns.md#sns-queue-policy-sourcearn-limits-to-one-topic) limits it to messages from this one topic.

options.text: Call the ConfirmSubscription API action for the subscription, because SNS delivers nothing to a queue until someone confirms the subscription.
options.why: When the queue and the topic are in the [same AWS account](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-same-account-sqs-subscription-needs-no-opt-in), the subscription needs no confirmation step.
options.misconception: A same-account queue subscription waits for a confirmation before SNS delivers.

options.text: Turn on raw message delivery for the subscription, because the subscription itself already gives the SNS service permission to send messages to the queue.
options.why: Raw delivery changes the message format; SNS still needs you to [set a policy on the Amazon SQS queue](../facts/sns.md#sns-sqs-queue-needs-policy-allowing-topic) that allows it to send.

items.explanation: A new queue's policy [allows only the queue owner](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-default-access-policy-owner-only) to send and receive messages, and SNS is not the owner. To publish from a topic to a queue you must [set a policy on the Amazon SQS queue](../facts/sns.md#sns-sqs-queue-needs-policy-allowing-topic). An [aws:SourceArn condition](../facts/sns.md#sns-queue-policy-sourcearn-limits-to-one-topic) lets messages from this one topic in and keeps every other sender out.
items.takeaway: SNS can send to a queue when the queue's policy allows the topic; limit that statement with aws:SourceArn.
items.twin: If the stem said "the queue is encrypted with a customer managed key" instead: also add a key policy statement, because SNS needs the [API actions GenerateDataKey and Decrypt](../facts/sns.md#sns-sse-topic-to-encrypted-queue-needs-cmk-policy).
items.say: The queue policy still allows only the owner, so I'd allow the SNS service with an aws:SourceArn condition for this topic.

solvers.stem_only: Subscribing through the API does not edit the queue policy; add a queue policy statement allowing sns.amazonaws.com sqs:SendMessage with an aws:SourceArn condition equal to the topic ARN.

items.stem: An application in account B runs on Amazon EC2 instances with an IAM role. The role's identity-based policy allows sqs:SendMessage on an Amazon SQS queue in account A. Every SendMessage call fails with an access denied error. The queue uses SSE-SQS encryption, and its access policy has not changed since the queue was created. Which solution grants access in the MOST secure way and follows the principle of least privilege?
keywords: its access policy has not changed

options.text: Add a statement to the queue's access policy in account A that allows the role's ARN to call sqs:SendMessage on this queue.
options.why: Across accounts the [resource-based policy in the trusting account must allow the requester](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-cross-account-needs-both-policies), and this statement names one role and one action.

options.text: Change the identity-based policy of the role in account B to allow sqs:* on all resources, so that the role can reach the queue.
options.why: Account A must [configure the queue's access policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-cross-account-needs-queue-access-policy) for the role, and sqs:* on every resource also breaks least privilege.

options.text: Add a statement to the queue's access policy in account A that allows every principal (*) to call sqs:SendMessage on this queue.
options.why: It works, but a wildcard principal lets principals of every AWS account send to the queue, which breaks least privilege.
options.misconception: Allows every principal when one role needs access.

options.text: Add a statement to the queue's access policy that allows the role's ARN, and remove sqs:SendMessage from the role's own policy.
options.why: AWS [allows the request only if both evaluations return Allow](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-cross-account-needs-both-policies), so the role's own permission must stay.

items.explanation: The role already has its allow in account B. The queue's policy [allows only the queue owner](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-default-access-policy-owner-only), so account A still denies the call. Account A must [configure the queue's access policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-cross-account-needs-queue-access-policy) to allow that principal, and a statement that names one role and one action grants exactly what the application needs.
items.takeaway: Cross-account access to a queue needs the queue's access policy to allow the principal, as well as the principal's own policy.
items.twin: If the stem said "the queue is in the same account as the role" instead: the call already succeeds, because [the permissions of identity-based and resource-based policies are a union](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-same-account-identity-or-resource-allow).
items.say: Account B already allows it, so I'd add the role's ARN to the queue policy in account A.

solvers.stem_only: Cross-account access needs both sides: keep the role's identity policy and add a queue policy statement in account A that allows the role ARN sqs:SendMessage on that queue only. SSE-SQS needs no KMS permissions.

citations: docs/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account#You must also attach an identity-based p

items.stem: An Amazon SNS topic delivers messages to an Amazon SQS queue in the same AWS account. The queue's access policy allows the topic to send messages. A new company rule requires the queue to be encrypted at rest with an AWS KMS key whose key policy the company controls. After the team turned on SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key for Amazon SQS, no messages arrive in the queue. Which TWO actions will restore delivery and meet the rule with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: AWS managed key for Amazon SQS

options.text: Edit the key policy of the AWS managed key for Amazon SQS so that it allows the SNS service principal to use the key.
options.why: You [cannot modify the key policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-kms-aws-managed-key-policy-not-modifiable) of the AWS managed KMS key for Amazon SQS, so no statement for SNS can be added.

options.text: Create a customer managed KMS key, and configure the queue to use this key for server-side encryption instead of the AWS managed key.
options.why: For AWS services that send to encrypted queues, you must [create a customer managed KMS key](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-kms-service-senders-need-customer-managed-key), and the company controls its key policy.

options.text: Switch the queue to SSE-SQS encryption, which uses keys that Amazon SQS manages, and keep the access policy of the queue unchanged.
options.why: SSE-SQS uses [SQS-managed encryption keys (SSE-SQS)](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-sse-two-key-types), so the company has no key policy to control, which the rule requires.
options.misconception: SSE-SQS gives the company a key policy that it controls.

options.text: Add a statement to the key policy of the new key that allows the SNS service principal to use kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt.
options.why: The key policy must grant SNS the [API actions GenerateDataKey and Decrypt](../facts/sns.md#sns-sse-topic-to-encrypted-queue-needs-cmk-policy), so that SNS can encrypt the messages that it sends.

options.text: Create a customer managed key in an AWS KMS custom key store that an AWS CloudHSM cluster backs, and configure the queue to use it.
options.why: It works with the key policy statement, but a CloudHSM cluster is extra hardware to run, although a standard customer managed key meets the rule.
options.misconception: A key policy that the company controls needs dedicated key hardware.

items.explanation: SNS needs the queue's KMS key to send to the encrypted queue. You [cannot modify the key policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-kms-aws-managed-key-policy-not-modifiable) of the AWS managed key, so the queue needs a customer managed key. Its key policy, which the company controls, must allow SNS the [API actions GenerateDataKey and Decrypt](../facts/sns.md#sns-sse-topic-to-encrypted-queue-needs-cmk-policy).
items.takeaway: An AWS service that sends to an SSE-KMS queue needs a customer managed key whose policy allows that service.
items.twin: If the stem said "S3 event notifications send the messages" instead: name the S3 service principal in the key policy, because event sources need [permissions in the key policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-kms-service-senders-need-customer-managed-key).
items.say: The AWS managed key's policy can't be changed, so I'd use a customer managed key and allow SNS in its key policy.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for TWO actions that restore delivery and meet the key rule with the LEAST operational overhead.

I mark the constraints: SNS sends to the queue, the queue's access policy already allows the topic, the company must control the key policy, and delivery stopped after SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key.
Before I look at the options, I predict one fix: edit the policy of the AWS managed key so that it allows the SNS service principal.
I remove SSE-SQS, because the company then controls no key policy. I remove the CloudHSM custom key store, because a standard customer managed key meets the rule with less to run.

Between editing the AWS managed key and creating a customer managed key the difference is who owns the key policy. My first idea breaks because the key policy of the AWS managed key for Amazon SQS cannot be modified; the stem says the company controls the key policy, so I choose a customer managed key and a statement that allows SNS to use GenerateDataKey and Decrypt.
Check: the new key and its policy statement restore delivery, the company controls the key policy, and the access policy of the queue stays as it is. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: The AWS managed key's policy cannot be edited, so SNS cannot use it. Create a customer managed KMS key for the queue and add a key policy statement that lets the SNS service principal use kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt.

items.stem: A company runs order-processing workers on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Several applications send messages to an Amazon SQS standard queue. The workers poll the queue and delete each message after they process it. Processing a message takes a few seconds. A few malformed messages fail every time, and the workers receive them again and again for days. Which change will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: A few malformed messages fail every time

options.text: Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to a value that is longer than the longest processing time of one message.
options.why: A longer timeout makes the workers [wait for a relatively long time](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-visibility-timeout-too-long-delays-retry) between attempts, but the malformed message still fails and comes back.

options.text: Create a dead-letter queue, and add a redrive policy to the queue that moves a message after several unsuccessful receives.
options.why: A [source queue can send messages](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-dlq-definition-isolate-unprocessable-messages) to its dead-letter queue when the consumer cannot process them, so the loop stops.

options.text: Change the workers to call ChangeMessageVisibility during processing, so that each message stays hidden until the worker finishes with it.
options.why: Extending the timeout from the workers delays each new attempt, but the malformed message still fails and returns to the queue.

options.text: Change the workers to count the receives of each message and to move a message that keeps failing to a second queue.
options.why: It works, but the workers then carry custom code for what a redrive policy on the queue does without code.
options.misconception: Builds in worker code what a redrive policy already does.

items.explanation: A malformed message fails every time, so it returns after each visibility timeout for days. A redrive policy sets the [number of times a consumer can receive](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning) a message; after that, SQS moves the message to the dead-letter queue. The workers stop receiving it, and the team can review it there.
items.takeaway: A message that fails every time needs a redrive policy and a dead-letter queue, not a longer timeout.
items.twin: If the stem said "many messages are processed by two different workers" instead: increase the visibility timeout, because the default of [30 seconds](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-visibility-timeout-default) ends during processing.
items.say: The same bad messages fail forever, so I'd add a redrive policy that moves them to a dead-letter queue.

solvers.stem_only: Poison messages: configure a dead-letter queue with a redrive policy (maxReceiveCount) on the source queue.

items.stem: A company runs an order API on Amazon EC2 instances. The API sends each order directly to the order service, which writes the order to a relational database. During sales, the database cannot keep up, requests time out, and orders are lost. The order service, the shipping service and the analytics service must each process every order. Each service must process every order, even after it has been offline for a few hours. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: even after it has been offline for a few hours

options.text: Have the API send each order to one Amazon SQS queue, and have each service that processes orders poll that queue and process the orders it receives.
options.why: A queue serves [a single subscriber typically](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss): three services that poll one queue split the orders, so each service misses most of them.

options.text: Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for each service that processes orders, and have each service poll its queue.
options.why: Each service gets its own queue with a copy of every order, and each queue holds the orders while its service is offline.

options.text: Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe the HTTPS endpoint of each service that processes orders so that each service receives every order.
options.why: In SNS, [messages are not persisted](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-no-persistence), and HTTPS retries end within [3,600 seconds](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-http-total-retry-time-max), so a service offline for hours loses orders.

options.text: Move the database to a larger instance class, and add a read replica so that the database can take more of the load during sales.
options.why: A larger database still takes every write at the moment of the peak, and it gives the shipping and analytics services no orders at all.
options.misconception: a larger database removes the need for messaging between the services

items.explanation: Three services each need every order, and each can be offline for hours. Each order published to the topic is [fanned out to the SQS queues](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-fanout-identical-messages-to-multiple-sqs-queues), one queue per service, and each queue keeps its copy until its service processes it. AWS uses this pattern to prevent message loss [when subscribers are offline](../facts/sns.md#sns-with-sqs-prevents-loss-for-offline-subscribers).
items.takeaway: Several consumers that each need every message and can go offline: SNS topic to one SQS queue each.
items.twin: If the stem said "Only the company's order service processes the orders" instead: one SQS queue that the order service polls, because one consumer needs no topic.
items.say: Every service needs every order and can be offline, so I fan out from an SNS topic to one SQS queue per service.

solvers.stem_only: SNS-to-SQS fan-out: publish each order to an SNS topic, subscribe one SQS queue per service; each queue buffers its service's copy while it is offline.

items.stem: A company runs an order system in which Amazon EC2 instances process messages from an Amazon SQS queue. On some nights the consumers stop working for a while, and customers notice late orders the next morning. The operations team wants to monitor the queue and receive an alarm when messages wait too long before a consumer processes them. Which Amazon CloudWatch metric should the alarm use?
keywords: messages wait too long before a consumer processes them

options.text: The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible metric of the queue
options.why: It counts messages [received but not yet deleted or expired](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-not-visible-messages-is-in-flight), so it shows work in progress, and stopped consumers receive nothing.

options.text: The NumberOfMessagesSent metric of the queue
options.why: It counts the messages that producers add to the queue, so it shows arrivals, not how long any message waits.
options.misconception: The number of arriving messages shows how long messages wait.

options.text: The ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage metric of the queue
options.why: It reports the age of the [oldest unprocessed message in the queue](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-age-of-oldest-message-measures-lag), which is the wait that the team wants to watch.

options.text: The CPUUtilization metric of the consumer instances
options.why: CPU shows how busy the instances are; stopped consumers use little CPU, so the alarm stays quiet when orders wait.
options.misconception: Instance CPU shows how long messages wait in a queue.

items.explanation: The team cares about how long messages wait, not how many arrive. [ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-age-of-oldest-message-measures-lag) reports the age of the oldest unprocessed message. When the consumers stop, that age grows, so an alarm on it fires whatever the number of instances.
items.takeaway: To alarm on waiting time, watch ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage; to scale workers, use the backlog per instance.
items.twin: If the stem said "scale the consumers so that the backlog stays small" instead: the [backlog per instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance), because a target tracking policy needs a value that moves with the group size.
items.say: Wait time is the age of the oldest message, so I'd alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage.

solvers.stem_only: Alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage of the queue.
